title: How to verify homeschool requirements by state
dek: Verify your homeschool route using official state sources and three limited examples. This is not an exhaustive 50-state legal summary.
metaDescription: Verify your homeschool route using official state sources and three limited examples. This is not an exhaustive 50-state legal summary.

paragraphs: To check homeschool requirements by state, identify your state and legal education route, then read the current education-department guidance and underlying law for that route. Write down what you must file, what you must retain, and what must be assessed. A state label such as low or high regulation is not a compliance checklist.

Perhaps a move, a first school withdrawal or an evaluator's request has made the paperwork suddenly feel urgent. The useful question is not how much another family keeps. It is what your route requires for this child, this school year and this deadline. This guide explains how to verify that, with selected official examples, not a certified 50-state legal table.

body.heading: Choose the route before copying the rule
paragraphs: Home education, enrollment in an umbrella or private school, public online schooling and tutoring arrangements can operate under different requirements. A child learning at the kitchen table is not necessarily legally homeschooled. Record the exact route name from the official page, along with compulsory-attendance age and any special provisions relevant to your child.

Then follow the state education agency's home-education page to its statute, regulations, forms and district contact. Check whether the page is current and whether a change is enacted law, proposed legislation or an old summary. A search-result excerpt can be a useful lead, but should not become your only record of a deadline.

body.heading: Build a requirement record you can actually use
items: Write the state, child's age or grade, education route and school year at the top. Do not copy a sibling's requirements without checking age and grade conditions.
Record the notice or application recipient, current form, filing trigger and deadline. Save submission evidence or acknowledgment where available.
List attendance, days, hours or subject requirements only where the relevant official rule calls for them. Keep the definition and counting period alongside the number.
Separate records retained at home from material submitted annually or produced on request. Those are different jobs, even when they concern the same portfolio.
Record assessment options, who can assess, covered grades, due date and where evidence goes. Do not assume a portfolio is required simply because it is one permitted option.
Find retention requirements and any rules for moving, ending a program or returning to school. Put a reminder before the next genuine deadline.
Save the official URL, access date and a copy of the instructions. List unanswered questions for the agency, district or qualified legal adviser.

body.heading: Selected official examples, not nationwide categories
columns: What to verify for your family
rows: Ohio
Section 3321.042 defines home education and sets notice and subject assurances; it does not impose the old annual assessment framework.
The notice trigger, superintendent recipient, current dates and whether this is your actual route.
Texas
TEA says it does not register, approve or regulate homeschool programs and explains transfer and assurance issues.
The applicable course-of-study obligations and records a future receiving school may need.
Florida
The education department identifies parent-directed home education and provides statute, parent-resource and district-contact routes.
The requirements for your particular home-education route, rather than a different scholarship or school arrangement.

body.heading: Ohio shows why old tables need checking
paragraphs: The [Ohio statute](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3321.042), effective October 2023, specifies notice and educational subject assurances. It states notice is due within five calendar days of specified starting, moving or withdrawal events, and by August 30 each year thereafter. Read its exact conditions before applying them to your situation. Do not carry forward an old Ohio row requiring annual testing or a portfolio review.

The [Texas agency page](https://tea.texas.gov/families-and-students/finding-school-your-child/home-schooling) demonstrates a different problem: little state filing does not mean there are no educational obligations or future transfer questions. The [Florida home-education page](https://www.fldoe.org/schools/school-choice/home-edu/) directs families to legal and district resources. Neither example establishes a rule for neighboring states.

body.heading: Invented example: moving between districts
paragraphs: A family using Ohio's home-education route moves to a new district in the middle of the year. Rather than assuming the previous acknowledgment covers the new address indefinitely, the parent checks the moving trigger in the statute, identifies the new superintendent and saves the new notice and response.

They also retain their child's ordinary learning notes and selected work. Those voluntary records help explain continuity, but are not relabelled as a legally required portfolio. If the move crossed a state line, they would check both the departure obligations and the destination route from scratch, not transfer an Ohio checklist unchanged.

body.heading: Keep, submit or choose
rows: Keep
You retain evidence for a stated period or possible review.
Storage location, retention rule and owner.
Submit
A recipient must receive a form, report or assessment.
Recipient, deadline, delivery method and proof.
Choose
The rule allows alternative assessments or routes.
Selected option and why the child qualifies.
Optional
You want the record for teaching, transfer or later applications.
Purpose and review date, not invented legal status.

body.heading: Ask for a precise clarification
paragraphs: Ask the official contact: We are using [route] for a child aged [age] in [district]. Please point me to the current rule for [specific record]. Must we keep it, submit it, or choose it as one assessment option? Which deadline and recipient apply?

If you need the agency contact, start with the [US Department of Education state contact directory](https://www.ed.gov/about/contact-us/state-contacts). It is a route to official offices, not a federal statement of each state's homeschool law.

body.heading: When a general guide is not enough
paragraphs: Pause before relying on a summary if sources conflict, a district requests something you cannot locate in the rule, the child has additional education needs, custody is disputed, or attendance enforcement has begun. Ask for the current written authority and obtain qualified advice where necessary. Do not ignore an official notice because an online chart says your state files nothing.

Keep a small voluntary record even when a particular legal portfolio is not required: what was studied, representative work, outside-provider records and any completed assessments. For a practical format, use [the record-keeping template guide](/guides/homeschool-record-keeping-template). More pages are not automatically stronger evidence, and an app cannot certify compliance from a state selection alone.

items.a: There is no single reliable answer without specifying the route and current law. A portfolio may be mandatory, one assessment option or simply useful family evidence. Check the state's official home-education instructions and underlying rule, then record whether the portfolio must be retained, submitted or made available for review.

items.q: Do I need to count homeschool days or hours?
items.a: Only the applicable rule can answer that for your route. Some systems use days, some hours, and some do not impose that kind of count. Do not copy a national number or another state's definition. Record the required period and what counts before setting up an attendance total.

items.q: Can I use this as a complete 50-state compliance chart?
items.a: No. This is a verification method with selected checked official examples, not an exhaustive legal survey. It intentionally avoids nationwide tier totals and unsupported rows. Build your own state-and-route record from current official instructions and ask for clarification when age, grade, enrollment or moving conditions change the answer.
